identity.title: The Art of Scaling Reinforcement Learning Compute for LLMs

problem.claim: Develop predictive and principled methods for evaluating and scaling reinforcement-learning compute for LLM training.

gap.claim: Existing RL scaling lacks the predictive methodologies and principled understanding available for pre-training.

contributions.claim: A framework for analyzing and predicting RL scaling in LLMs using compute-performance curves and design-choice ablations.
A large-scale study of RL scaling covering more than 400,000 GPU-hours.
ScaleRL, a proposed best-practice recipe for scalable RL training and validation-performance prediction.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors characterize the study as the first large-scale systematic analysis defining a principled framework for RL scaling in LLMs.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that recipes differ in asymptotic performance, while loss aggregation, normalization, curriculum, and off-policy algorithm mainly affect compute efficiency without materially shifting the asymptote.
The authors report that stable, scalable recipes follow predictable trajectories, allowing extrapolation from smaller-scale runs.
The authors report successfully scaling and predicting validation performance in a single RL run using up to 100,000 GPU-hours.

narrative_sequence.summary: RL is central to LLM training, but predictive scaling methods comparable to pre-training are lacking.
The abstract identifies no principled way to evaluate algorithmic improvements as RL compute grows.
The study fits sigmoidal compute-performance curves and ablates common design choices to separate asymptotic performance from compute efficiency.
Reported scaling patterns motivate the ScaleRL recipe, which is demonstrated on a 100,000-GPU-hour RL run.

source_observation.claim: The abstract distinguishes design choices that shift asymptotic performance from those that primarily change compute efficiency, and uses scaling trajectories to support extrapolation.

lessons.interpretation: Separating endpoint quality from resource efficiency can make scaling claims more diagnostic and comparable.
lessons.application: Report each intervention against both an estimated asymptote and compute-to-performance trajectory, then state which quantity changes.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the task has no meaningful asymptotic regime or when compute-performance curves cannot be estimated reliably.

unknowns: S5 lacks the numbering marker (2), but includes an intervening observation about design choices primarily affecting compute efficiency; the supplied abstract does not establish whether any substantive content is missing.
It does not specify the LLMs, RL tasks, validation metric, baselines, curve-fitting procedure, prediction error, or evidence supporting the claimed effectiveness.
The abstract does not quantify how much each design choice changes asymptotic performance or compute efficiency.
